newsitem.title: UK: U.S. seen bowing to inevitable on Internet trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen bowing to inevitable on Internet trade.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
President Bill Clinton's call for global free trade on the Internet is a realistic way to embrace a phenomenon that threatened to escape government control anyway, industry experts said on Wednesday.
But not all countries will favour the plan.

Some European governments would still seek to tax and regulate electronic commerce but that would achieve nothing and just be worse for their citizens, said Dr Madsen Pirie of the Adam Smith Institute, a right-wing think-tank.

Other experts said recruiting the World Trade Organisation (WTO) would help create an infrastructure for electronic commerce and minimise inevitable tax revenue losses from trading between firms and individuals which could seek to avoid higher tax areas.
Business transacted across the Internet, the world-wide network of personal computers linked by telephone lines, is expected to explode over the next few years.
This electronic commerce will be led by people sitting at home doing banking, ordering books, groceries, holidays and CDs from their computer screens.
The danger to governments is that cybernauts can view price lists and taxes on goods right across the world and will inevitably buy where both are lowest, the experts said.
According to U.S. high-technology research company IDG, more than one billion people across the world will be users of personal computers by 2000, up from 450 million in 1996.
On Tuesday Clinton hailed the Internet as an engine for future economic growth and unveiled a largely laissez-faire policy to promote it.
He said the WTO should declare the Internet a global free-trade zone.

"This is excellent news. It is going with the grain of what is happening, instead of trying to stick fingers and thumbs in the dyke of electronic commerce. This recognises it is going to happen," said Pirie.
"There will be European countries which try to regulate and tax electronic commerce and they will lose out to countries which do not and take a more enlightened attitude," said Pirie.

Bill Thompson, managing director of Internet commerce consultantcy Mocha Ltd, said the Clinton plan was a good public relations way of admitting that governments would not be able to tax and control future electronic commerce.
"Clinton is really trying to make sure the government doesn't lose all control and the tax base is not eroded too much.
"They want to build an infrastructure to persuade Internet business to come on board and make sure tax revenues won't disappear when the cyber-economic growth hits top gear," Thompson said.

Professor Alan Cawson of Sussex University in the south of England said Clinton was right to point out some of existing barriers which needed to be overcome, like payment security, intellectual property rights and the need to protect children from pornography.
And the idea of a global trade-free zone could bury forever the idea, recently floating around the European Union, that a "byte" tax should be imposed on traffic across the Internet.
David Birch, director of information technology consultancy Hyperion, also welcomed what he said was the realism behind Clinton's plan.

"It shows he's looked at the problem (of future tax revenue) and realised that nothing can be done to impose things like taxes, so the best thing to do is accept the inevitable and get on with it," Birch said.
